Ottawa Temperature and Atmospheric Teleconnection Indices

An 85-year analysis of NAO, AO, PDO, and ENSO relationships with Ottawa (1940–2024)

Author

John Lewis - “Climate Analysis — Ottawa”

Published

May 26, 2026

:::

1 Introduction

Large-scale patterns of ocean and atmospheric circulation — known as teleconnection indices — can modulate regional climate conditions thousands of kilometres away. For Ottawa, ON, a continental mid-latitude city with pronounced seasonal temperature swings, these remote forcings may contribute meaningfully to year-to-year and decade-to-decade variability on top of the long-term warming trend.

This report examines the statistical relationship between Ottawa’s surface air temperatures (1940–2024) and four major teleconnection indices:

  • NAO — North Atlantic Oscillation: pressure seesaw between the Icelandic Low and Azores High
  • AO — Arctic Oscillation: annular mode of polar vs. mid-latitude pressure-sometimes referred to as the Polar Vortex
  • PDO — Pacific Decadal Oscillation: multi-decadal SST pattern in the North Pacific
  • ENSO — El Niño–Southern Oscillation (via the Oceanic Niño Index): tropical Pacific SST anomalies

For each index, the analysis focuses on two temporal scales: annual means and winter (December–January–February, DJF) seasonal means, since winter is when teleconnection signals tend to be strongest at mid-latitudes.

2 Data

2.1 Data sources

Variable Source Period Resolution
Ottawa temperature Environment Canada (OTTAWA MACDONALD-CARTIER INT’L A) 1940–2024 Daily
NAO NOAA CPC (nao.monthly1.txt, extended 1940–1949) 1940–2024 Monthly
AO NOAA CPC (ao_y.f2.csv) + UsingR::arctic.oscillations (1940–1949) 1940–2024 Monthly
PDO NOAA CPC (pdo1940.csv) 1940–2024 Monthly
ONI (ENSO) NOAA CPC (online, oni.ascii.txt) 1950–2024 3-month running mean

Temperature anomalies are computed as deviations from the 1940–2024 monthly climatological mean for each calendar month. Winter seasons span December–January–February (DJF), with December associated with the following calendar year (e.g., December 1999 belongs to Winter 2000).

3 Ottawa temperature overview

The LOESS curve reveals a clear upward trend in both annual and winter temperatures over the 85-year record, with the most pronounced warming occurring from the 1980s onward. Year-to-year variability in winter temperatures remains substantial, suggesting a role for large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns on top of the underlying warming trend.

4 North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)

4.1 What is the NAO?

The NAO is defined by the pressure difference between the Icelandic Low and the Azores High. A positive NAO drives stronger westerlies, bringing mild, wet conditions to northwestern Europe and typically milder winters to eastern North America. A negative NAO allows cold Arctic air to penetrate further south, producing colder winters in eastern Canada and the northeastern United States.

4.2 NAO index over time

4.3 NAO vs. Ottawa winter temperature

The NAO shows a modest positive correlation with Ottawa winter temperatures (r ≈ 0.29), accounting for roughly 8% of winter temperature variance. The rolling correlation reveals that this relationship has not been stable over time — there are multi-decadal periods of stronger and weaker coupling.

5 Arctic Oscillation (AO)

5.1 What is the AO?

The AO is the leading mode of sea-level pressure variability in the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. It is closely related to the NAO but captures a more annular (wave or ring-like) structure around the Arctic. A positive AO strengthens the polar vortex and keeps cold Arctic air bottled up at high latitudes, favouring mild winters in mid-latitude cities like Ottawa. A negative AO weakens the polar vortex and allows cold outbreaks to surge equatorward.

5.2 AO index over time

5.3 AO vs. Ottawa winter temperature

The AO shows a positive correlation with Ottawa winter temperatures (r ≈ 0.19), explaining roughly 4% of winter temperature variance. The rolling correlation on monthly data reveals periods of stronger and weaker coupling, reflecting the non-stationary nature of AO’s influence at this location.

6 Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO)

6.1 What is the PDO?

The PDO is a pattern of sea surface temperature variability in the North Pacific Ocean that oscillates on multi-decadal timescales (roughly 20–30 years per phase). Unlike ENSO, which operates on interannual timescales, the PDO represents longer-term “regime shifts.” A positive PDO (warm North Pacific coast, cool central Pacific) is associated with warmer-than-average winters across much of North America; a negative PDO tends to be associated with cooler conditions. The PDO may amplify or suppress ENSO teleconnections.

6.2 PDO regime over time

6.3 PDO vs. Ottawa winter temperature

The PDO shows a weaker correlation with Ottawa winter temperatures (r ≈ -0.27) than the AO or NAO. Its primary relevance for Ottawa may be through multi-decadal modulation of background conditions rather than direct year-to-year forcing.

7 El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO)

7.1 What is ENSO?

ENSO is the dominant mode of interannual climate variability on Earth, originating in the tropical Pacific. El Niño events (warm phase, ONI ≥ +0.5°C) and La Niña events (cool phase, ONI ≤ −0.5°C) teleconnect to mid-latitudes by altering jet stream positioning and stormtrack patterns. For eastern Canada, El Niño winters tend to be milder than average and La Niña winters tend to be cooler. The ONI (Oceanic Niño Index) is the 3-month running mean of SST anomalies in the Niño-3.4 region; data are available from NOAA from 1950 onward.

7.2 ONI index over time

7.3 Ottawa winter temperature by ENSO phase

ENSO, as measured by the DJF ONI, shows a positive relationship with Ottawa winter temperatures (r ≈ 0.18). El Niño winters in Ottawa tend to be warmer than average, while La Niña winters show a modest cold tendency. However, the spread within each phase is large, indicating that other factors (particularly the AO and NAO) play an important role in any given winter.

8 Multi-index comparison

8.1 Summary of correlations

8.2 Side-by-side winter scatter panels

8.3 Winter Cross Correlation

If ccf(temp, index), has a significant spike at a negative lag, this indicates that the atmospheric index leads the Ottawa temperature. A spike at zero indicates simultaneous co-variation.

Notice that some of those indices (especially the NAO and AO) show very similar lag patterns. This occurs often because they are physically coupled by essentially different ways of measuring the same broad atmospheric pressure variations. There is a significant correlation value at lag 0 for NAO teleconnection as was noted previously. the NAO or AO correlations are much stronger (taller bars) in the winter version. This is because the jet stream is more active and “coupled” with the surface temperature in Ottawa during the colder months, whereas in the summer, local heating often drowns out those big teleconnection signals. Another observation of this data is the significant negative correlation at lag 0 for the PDO, where as with ENSO a negative correlation at lag 1 and 2 for previous winters, means that as the index goes up, Ottawa’s temperature goes down. This is common with ENSO in certain regions of Canada where the “seesaw” effect (teleconnections) can flip depending on the strength of the Pacific Jet Stream.

Reminder: In a winter-only dataset, Lag 1 is still 1 year (the previous winter). If the data are strictly sequential winters (1941, 1942, etc.), ccf will show how last year’s index correlates with this year’s temperature anomaly.

8.4 Annual anomaly co-variation

8.5 Highlights of the Annual Cross Correlation

The Atlantic “Lull” (NAO & AO):

The 8-9 Year Peak: Since Ottawa is inland, the direct “year-to-year” impact of the North Atlantic Oscillation is often messier than it is on the coast. That 8-9 year signal is a classic signature of decadal variability. It suggests that while the NAO doesn’t dictate if next year will be hot or cold, there is a decadal “rhythm” where the Atlantic pressure systems sync up with Ontario/Quebec temperatures over longer cycles.

In the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Valley region, the NAO and AO usually exert their strongest influence on the jet stream during the cold season. By isolating the winter months, as was done previously, those 8-9 year correlations strengthen, and even the significant correlations at lag 0 are “diluted” by the summer data.

Pacific Dominance (PDO & ENSO):

The 0 and 1-year Lag: The “very significant” negative correlation at lag 0/1 for PDO and ENSO suggests these are the primary drivers for Ottawa’s interannual temperature variability. In Eastern Canada, the positive phase of PDO and El Niño(positive ONI) typically bring warmer winters. Also, a significal correlation exists at ~8 years for the ENSO as was the case for NAO and AO.

9 Discussion and conclusions

Over the 85-year record, all four teleconnection indices show a statistically positive relationship with Ottawa winter temperatures, meaning that warm-phase conditions in each index are associated, on average, with warmer winters in Ottawa. However, the strength of these relationships varies considerably:

  • AO and NAO are the most directly coupled to Ottawa winter variability. Both describe the state of the polar vortex and Atlantic pressure systems that steer cold Arctic air into or away from eastern Canada. Detrended winter correlations with Ottawa temperatures are r ≈ 0.12 (AO) and r ≈ 0.13 (NAO). The rolling correlation analysis reveals that neither relationship has been stable over time, with multi-decadal periods of stronger and weaker coupling.

  • ENSO provides a moderate teleconnection signal (r ≈ 0.2 detrended). El Niño winters tend to be milder and La Niña winters colder on average, but within-phase variability is large — any given winter can deviate substantially from the phase composite mean, largely because the AO and NAO can override or reinforce the ENSO signal.

  • PDO shows the weakest direct correlation, in fact negative, with Ottawa winter temperatures (r ≈ -0.24 detrended), consistent with its role as a lower-frequency modulator rather than a direct driver of interannual variability. Its primary influence may be in conditioning the background state that either amplifies or suppresses ENSO teleconnections. The PDO operates on much longer timescales than ENSO, with regimes that can persist for decades, so its year-to-year climate effects are more muted.

The lag relationship between Ottawa temperature anomalies, for both annual and winter periods, and the four different indices indicate that there are specific phase date relationships that are statistically significant.

Taken together, no single index provides strong predictive power for a given Ottawa winter. These indices often “sleep” in the summer but dominate the weather patterns in the winter months. The year-to-year variability in winter temperatures reflects the combined and often competing influences of all these circulation patterns, plus a chaotic weather variability. Future analysis could examine combined multi-index models and the non-stationarity of these teleconnections under anthropogenic climate change.

Data sources: Environment Canada (Ottawa temperature); NOAA Climate Prediction Center (NAO, AO, PDO, ONI); UsingR R package (historical AO, 1940–1949).
